overview.title: Why text augmentation is hard, and the idea of pretraining a word embedding
overview.main_topic: The end of the "Augmenting text data" sidebar (deleting/swapping words, its pitfalls, generative augmentation) and the start of section 14.5.4: pretraining as the dominant NLP approach, using the IMDb unsup/ reviews, and introducing the Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW) model
overview.central_idea: Text augmentation is brittle because language is order-dependent and small edits can change meaning, so it is usually better to find more text. A better way to use extra unlabeled text is pretraining: an unsupervised task (here CBOW, predicting a word from its neighbors) trains the Embedding layer's parameters before the model is specialized to the labeled classification task.
overview.importance: It explains the fix for the problem diagnosed on p.437, where the LSTM with a learned Embedding stalled at about 84% because 20,000 labeled reviews are not enough to learn good embeddings. Pretraining on unlabeled text is the idea behind word2vec, BERT (p.479) and modern LLMs.
learning_objectives: Describe basic text-augmentation edits (deleting and swapping words) and why they are risky
Contrast the robustness of image augmentation with the order-sensitivity of text
Explain why the authors recommend collecting more text rather than investing in text augmentation
Define pretraining and explain why large sequence models need it
Explain how an unsupervised task can train parameters without labels
State the plan of section 14.5.4: pretrain the Embedding layer on all IMDb reviews, including unsup/, with CBOW
prerequisites: Word embeddings and the Embedding layer (pp.433-436)
The LSTM classifier and its 84% plateau (p.437)
The IMDb dataset preparation, including the ignored unsup/ directory (p.420)

summary:
The page opens with the end of the sidebar **"Augmenting text data"**, begun on p.437. Basic augmentation edits text to make a model more robust: randomly delete words or swap their positions, so "The rain in Spain falls mainly on the plain" becomes "The rain Spain falls plain on the mainly." Training on such edited inputs can make a model robust to typos and grammar mistakes. But the example also shows the **big pitfall**: it is easy to change the meaning of an example by accident. A cat photo is still a cat after cropping, rotating or recoloring. Language, by contrast, is **order-dependent and highly sensitive to tiny changes**, and swapping two words can reverse a sentence's meaning. Replacing words with synonyms from a table is also brittle, because a word can have several meanings and the wrong one may be picked. For these reasons text augmentation is not widespread, and the authors advise that **it is usually better to seek more text examples**. They add that generative models (coming chapters) offer a new kind of augmentation: generating new, coherent inputs that plausibly resemble the data, useful where data is sparse.

**Section 14.5.4** then introduces **pretraining**, which has been the dominant approach to text modeling during the last decade of NLP progress. Sequence models with millions or billions of parameters are very data-hungry, and labeled examples are usually the bottleneck. The idea is to design an **unsupervised task** that trains parameters without labels, on text from a similar domain or on arbitrary text in the target languages. This "primes" the model with general patterns of language before it is specialized to the final task.

Word embeddings were one of the first big successes of pretraining. The authors recall the `unsup/` directory of IMDb that was ignored earlier: it holds another 25,000 reviews, the same size as the training data. They will combine all of this text and pretrain the parameters of an `Embedding` layer with an unsupervised task. The setup is the **Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW)** model (Mikolov et al., 2013, footnote 2): slide a window over the text and guess the missing middle word from its neighbors (the sentence continues on p.439).

paragraphs.excerpt: or swap the position of words in a sentence, so the sentence
paragraphs.what_it_says: This finishes the list of basic augmentation edits begun on p.437 ("we might randomly delete" ... "or swap the position of words"). The example turns "The rain in Spain falls mainly on the plain" into "The rain Spain falls plain on the mainly." Training on such edited inputs can make the model robust to typos and grammar mistakes.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The example applies both edits: "in" is deleted, and "mainly" and "plain" swap places. The perturbed sentence imitates the noisy text real users write (missing words, wrong order), so a model that has seen such noise during training is less likely to fail on it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the text version of the image augmentation the reader already knows: random, label-preserving edits that enlarge the effective training set.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Augmentation assumes the label is invariant under the transformation. Deletion and swaps are cheap, random transformations applied on the fly at training time.

terminology.meaning: Creating modified copies of training texts (deletions, swaps, synonym replacement, generated text) to make a model more robust.
A model's ability to keep predicting correctly when inputs are noisy or slightly different from the training data.

connections: p.437: the sidebar starts there, motivated by the importance of data augmentation for computer vision.

paragraphs.excerpt: However, this example also concisely shows the big pitfall with text augmentation
paragraphs.what_it_says: The same example shows the main danger: you can easily change the meaning of an input by accident. You can crop, rotate and recolor a cat picture and still have a recognizable cat, but language is order-dependent and very sensitive to tiny changes, and a sentence with two words swapped might mean the opposite. Replacing words with synonyms from a table is also brittle if the wrong sense of a word is chosen. So text augmentation is not widespread, and it is usually better to look for more text examples than to spend time on augmentation techniques.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Image augmentations act on continuous pixel values and are chosen to keep the object's identity. Text is discrete and compositional: meaning comes from which words appear and in what order. "The movie was not good, it was great" and "The movie was good, it was not great" contain the same words but differ in sentiment. A synonym table that maps "fine" to "penalty" in "the acting was fine" produces nonsense, because "fine" has several senses. An augmentation that flips or corrupts the label adds noise instead of signal.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is practical advice: for text, effort is better spent gathering data, and this leads directly into pretraining, which uses extra unlabeled text instead of synthetic edits.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Image transformations like small rotations are (approximately) label-preserving symmetries of the data. Edits to word order have no such guarantee, because the label depends on syntax.

terminology.meaning: The meaning depends on the order of the elements, not only on which elements are present.
An augmentation that swaps words for synonyms from a lookup table; it breaks when a word is polysemous (has several meanings).

connections: p.419: sets vs. sequences, where word order was introduced as the key difference between the two model families.
p.437: augmentation for vision is recalled at the start of the sidebar.

paragraphs.excerpt: Generative models, which we will see in the coming chapters, are beginning
paragraphs.what_it_says: Generative models, covered in the coming chapters, are starting to offer a new form of text augmentation. A model that has learned to produce consistent, coherent text can generate completely unseen inputs that plausibly resemble the input data. This has its own challenges but opens a new frontier where data is sparse and hard to collect.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Instead of corrupting real examples, you ask a language model to write new examples (for example, new movie reviews with a given sentiment). Because the generator writes fluent text, the meaning-destroying problem of random edits is reduced.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It points forward to language models (chapter 15) and text generation with LLMs (chapter 16), and to the now-common practice of training small models on synthetic data.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the "own challenges" include generated examples whose label is wrong, low diversity (the generator repeats similar phrasings), and copying the generator's biases.

terminology.meaning: A model trained to produce new data (here, text) that resembles its training data.
Training examples produced by a model or program rather than collected from the real world.

connections: p.446: chapter 15 starts with the language model, which generates text.
p.524: chapter 16 goes further with LLMs.

paragraphs.excerpt: The last decade of rapid advancement in NLP has coincided with the
paragraphs.what_it_says: The last decade of fast progress in NLP has coincided with the rise of pretraining as the dominant approach. When we move from simple set-based regression models to sequence models with millions or billions of parameters, text models become extremely data-hungry, and we are usually limited by our ability to find labeled examples for a particular problem.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The bag-of-words and bigram models of section 14.4 have few parameters and learn from simple counts, so 20,000 labels are enough. An LSTM with an Embedding layer must learn a vector for every word and complex order-dependent patterns, which needs far more examples than any single labeled dataset gives. Labels are expensive (someone has to annotate each review), but raw text is almost free.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This names the bottleneck behind p.437's result: the LSTM overfit (99% train accuracy) before it had learned good embeddings.

terminology.meaning: Training a model's parameters on a large, usually unlabeled dataset with a generic task before training (fine-tuning) on the task of interest.
Needing many training examples to generalize, typical of models with many parameters.
The book's name for the bag-of-words and bigram models of section 14.4, which ignore word order and apply logistic regression on top of a multi-hot vector.

connections: p.437: the LSTM with an Embedding layer plateaus around 84% and overfits.
p.423: the bag-of-words model that performs better with far fewer parameters.

paragraphs.excerpt: The idea is to devise an unsupervised task to train model parameters
paragraphs.what_it_says: The idea is to design an unsupervised task that trains model parameters without labeled data. The pretraining data can be text from a domain similar to the final task, or just arbitrary text in the languages of interest. Pretraining learns general patterns of language and so "primes" the model before it is specialized to the final task.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The trick is to build the labels from the text itself: hide part of the text and ask the model to predict it. Every sentence then yields training examples for free. What the model learns this way (which words appear in similar contexts, basic grammar) is useful for almost any downstream task, so those parameters are a better starting point than random initialization.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the pretrain-then-specialize recipe that the rest of the text chapters build on: CBOW here, masked language modeling for BERT and RoBERTa (p.479), and next-word prediction for GPT-style models.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: such tasks are often called self-supervised, since the targets come from the input itself. The book uses the word "unsupervised" because no human labels are involved.

terminology.meaning: A training objective whose targets come from unlabeled data, for example predicting a hidden word.
The task we actually care about (here, positive/negative review classification), learned after pretraining.
The book's word for giving a model useful initial parameters before task-specific training.

connections: p.479: BERT's masked language modeling is another unsupervised pretraining task.
p.444: the chapter summary restates that pretraining gets around the data-hungry nature of sequence models.

paragraphs.excerpt: Word embeddings were one of the first big successes with text pretraining
paragraphs.what_it_says: Word embeddings were one of the first big successes of text pretraining, and this section shows how to pretrain one. The unsup/ directory ignored during IMDb preparation contains another 25,000 reviews, the same size as the training data. All this text will be combined to pretrain the parameters of an Embedding layer with an unsupervised task.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The unsup/ reviews have no labels, so they were useless for the classifier, but they are ideal for an unsupervised task. Together with the labeled reviews (whose labels are simply ignored during pretraining), the pretraining corpus is about twice as large as before. Only the Embedding layer's weight matrix (vocabulary size x 64 on p.439) is pretrained; the LSTM will still be trained on labeled data afterward (p.442).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows that even a modest amount of extra unlabeled in-domain text can be put to use, which addresses the data shortage diagnosed on p.437.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Transfer at the level of one layer: the pretrained embedding matrix is copied into the classifier's Embedding layer, as later shown in section 14.5.5 (p.442).

terminology.meaning: The folder of the IMDb download with 25,000 reviews that have no sentiment label.
A Keras layer holding a trainable matrix with one vector per token ID; looking up rows maps token IDs to dense vectors.

connections: p.420: the IMDb dataset was loaded and unsup/ was set aside.
p.434: the Embedding layer was introduced as a replacement for one-hot encoding.
p.442: section 14.5.5 uses the pretrained embedding for classification.

paragraphs.excerpt: One of the most straightforward setups for training a word embedding is
paragraphs.what_it_says: One of the simplest setups for training a word embedding is the Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW) model (footnote 2: Mikolov et al., "Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space," ICLR 2013). The idea is to slide a window over all the text (the sentence continues on p.439: guess a missing word from the words directly to its left and right).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The context words are treated as an unordered "bag", which is why the model is called a bag of words. It is "continuous" because the context is represented by dense, continuous vectors (embeddings) rather than discrete counts. To predict the middle word well, words that appear in similar contexts must get similar vectors.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: CBOW is the concrete unsupervised task used in this section; pp.439-441 implement it with a window of nine tokens and 64-dimensional embeddings.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: Mikolov et al. introduced two word2vec architectures, CBOW (context predicts the word) and skip-gram (the word predicts its context). The book uses CBOW.

terminology.meaning: A shallow model that predicts a word from the average of its surrounding words' embeddings.
The fixed span of neighboring tokens around a target position used as the input.

connections: p.439: figure 14.6 and the nine-token windows of Listing 14.27.
p.423: the bag-of-words idea from set models, here used for context words.

concepts.name: Text data augmentation
concepts.definition: Making modified copies of training texts, for example by randomly deleting or swapping words, replacing words with synonyms, or generating new examples with a generative model.
concepts.intuition: It shows the model the kind of noise it will meet in practice, such as typos and slightly wrong grammar.
concepts.technical: It assumes the label is invariant under the edit. For text this assumption often fails, because meaning depends on word order and word sense.
concepts.significance: The book concludes it is not widespread and that more real data is usually the better investment.
concepts.example: "The rain in Spain falls mainly on the plain" -> "The rain Spain falls plain on the mainly."
concepts.misconception: Augmentation is not equally effective in every domain. What works for images (crop, rotate, recolor) has no safe equivalent for text.

concepts.name: Pretraining
concepts.definition: Training model parameters on an unsupervised task over large amounts of unlabeled text, before specializing the model to the final task.
concepts.intuition: The model first reads a lot of text to learn how language works in general, and only then learns the specific job.
concepts.technical: The targets come from the text itself (a hidden word), so every window of text is a training example. The learned weights initialize the task model.
concepts.significance: The dominant approach in NLP over the last decade, because large sequence models are data-hungry and labeled data is scarce.
concepts.example: Pretraining an Embedding layer with CBOW on the 25,000 unsup/ reviews plus the labeled reviews.
concepts.misconception: Pretraining data does not need to come from the final task; arbitrary text in the same language also helps.

concepts.name: Word embedding
concepts.definition: A learned dense vector for each token in the vocabulary, stored as the weight matrix of an Embedding layer.
concepts.intuition: Words used in similar ways end up close to each other in the vector space.
concepts.technical: An Embedding layer of shape (vocab_size, 64) maps token IDs to rows; its weights can be trained jointly with a task or pretrained separately.
concepts.significance: On p.437, embeddings learned jointly from 20,000 labeled reviews were not good enough; pretraining is the proposed fix.
concepts.example: In the book's run, the LSTM with a jointly trained embedding reached about 84% test accuracy (p.437).
concepts.misconception: A poor embedding result does not mean embeddings are useless; it may only mean too little training data, as the authors stress on p.437.

concepts.name: Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW)
concepts.definition: An unsupervised setup that slides a window over text and predicts each window's middle word from the surrounding words.
concepts.intuition: Like a fill-in-the-blank exercise: "sail, wave, mast" suggest "boat" (p.439).
concepts.technical: Context embeddings are averaged (order is ignored, hence "bag") and a softmax over the vocabulary predicts the target word. The embedding matrix is what we keep.
concepts.significance: One of the simplest and most influential word-embedding methods (word2vec, Mikolov et al. 2013).
concepts.example: With nine-token windows (p.439), the eight outer words predict the middle one.
concepts.misconception: CBOW's goal is not the word predictor itself; the predictor is thrown away and only the embeddings are reused.

concepts.name: Unsupervised (self-supervised) pretraining task
concepts.definition: A training objective built from unlabeled data, where the target is part of the input itself.
concepts.intuition: Hide something in the text and ask the model to recover it.
concepts.technical: Examples: CBOW (middle word from neighbors), masked language modeling (p.479), next-token prediction (chapter 15).
concepts.significance: It turns cheap raw text into unlimited training examples.
concepts.example: Each position of each IMDb review yields one (context, target) pair.
concepts.misconception: "Unsupervised" here does not mean there is no loss or target; the targets exist but come from the text, not from human annotators.

deeper.title: Why the swapped sentence can flip meaning
deeper.body:
Some word-order edits that are harmless for a bag-of-words model change the meaning entirely:

- "The dog bit the man" vs. "The man bit the dog": same words, different event.
- "Not bad, actually good" vs. "Not good, actually bad": same words, opposite sentiment.

An augmentation that randomly swaps two words would produce the second sentence of each pair from the first and keep the original label, which teaches the model the wrong thing. This is the problem the sidebar describes when it says a sentence with two words swapped might mean the opposite. (Examples are ours, not from the book.)

deeper.title: Learning a language before taking an exam
deeper.body: Training the LSTM only on 20,000 labeled reviews is like learning a foreign language only from the questions of one exam: you memorize the answers (99% train accuracy) without really understanding the words. Pretraining is like first reading many books in that language without any answers attached; when you then study for the exam, you already know what the words mean.

deeper.title: How much data the pretraining task gets
deeper.body: Beyond the book, a rough count: IMDb reviews average a few hundred tokens. With the 25,000 labeled training reviews plus 25,000 unsup/ reviews, about 50,000 reviews x roughly 250 tokens is on the order of 10 million windows, each a (context, middle word) training pair. The classifier, by contrast, gets one label per review (20,000 after the validation split). The same text gives hundreds of times more training targets for the embedding when the targets come from the text itself.

deeper.title: Where this leads
deeper.body:
1. p.439: build a TextVectorization layer with the same vocabulary but no padding, and cut the text into nine-token windows (middle word = label, eight neighbors = context).
2. pp.440-441: train a shallow CBOW model whose Embedding layer has 64 dimensions.
3. p.442: copy the pretrained embedding weights into the LSTM classifier.
4. p.443: the LSTM rises to roughly the level of the set-based models, still limited by the amount of ordered training data, which motivates the Transformer in chapter 15.

misconceptions.claim: Data augmentation works as well for text as for images.
misconceptions.correction: The book says it is not nearly as effective for text: language is order-dependent and small edits can change or reverse meaning, while image edits like crops keep the object recognizable.

misconceptions.claim: Synonym replacement is a safe text augmentation.
misconceptions.correction: It is brittle when the wrong meaning of a word is chosen from the synonym table.

misconceptions.claim: Pretraining requires labeled data from the final task.
misconceptions.correction: Pretraining uses an unsupervised task; the data can be similar-domain text or arbitrary text in the target language.

misconceptions.claim: The LSTM's 84% shows word embeddings do not help classification.
misconceptions.correction: The authors attribute it to too little data for learning embeddings jointly; pretraining on more text addresses this (p.437).

takeaways: Basic text augmentation deletes or swaps words to build robustness to typos and grammar mistakes.
Its big pitfall is changing meaning by accident, because language is order-dependent; synonym tables are brittle too.
The authors recommend seeking more text rather than investing in text augmentation; generative models may offer a new kind of augmentation.
Pretraining on an unsupervised task is the dominant NLP approach because large sequence models are data-hungry and labels are scarce.
Section 14.5.4 pretrains the Embedding layer on all IMDb text, including the 25,000 unlabeled unsup/ reviews, using CBOW (Mikolov et al. 2013).

questions.question: According to the sidebar, why has text augmentation not become widespread?
options: Edits easily change an example's meaning because language is order-dependent and sensitive to small changes
Augmented text makes models less robust to typos
Keras has no text augmentation layers
questions.answer: Edits easily change an example's meaning because language is order-dependent and sensitive to small changes
questions.explanation: The book names unintentional meaning changes as the big pitfall. Text is easy to edit, the book says augmentation can improve robustness to typos, and nothing is said about Keras layers.

questions.question: What two edits turn "The rain in Spain falls mainly on the plain" into "The rain Spain falls plain on the mainly"?
questions.answer: The word "in" is deleted, and "mainly" and "plain" are swapped.
questions.explanation: The sidebar lists random deletion (p.437) and swapping (p.438); the example shows both at once.

questions.question: Why is cropping a cat photo a safer augmentation than swapping two words in a review?
questions.answer: A cropped or rotated cat is still recognizably a cat, so the label is preserved; swapping words can change the meaning of a sentence, even to its opposite, so the label may no longer be correct.
questions.explanation: This is the contrast the book draws between image and text data.

questions.question: What makes pretraining possible without labeled data?
options: Using the test set as training data
An unsupervised task whose targets come from the text itself, such as guessing a missing word
Using one-hot encoding instead of embeddings
questions.answer: An unsupervised task whose targets come from the text itself, such as guessing a missing word
questions.explanation: The book: devise an unsupervised task to train parameters that do not need labeled data. Using the test set would be leakage, and the other two options are unrelated to pretraining.

questions.question: What is in the IMDb unsup/ directory, and why is it useful now when it was ignored before?
questions.answer: 25,000 unlabeled reviews. They were useless for supervised classification but can be used for the unsupervised CBOW task that pretrains the Embedding layer.
questions.explanation: The page reminds the reader of unsup/ and says all the text will be combined for pretraining.

questions.question: Connect this page to p.437: what problem does pretraining the embedding address?
questions.answer: With only 20,000 labeled reviews, the LSTM overfit (over 99% train accuracy) before learning good word embeddings and stalled near 84%. Pretraining learns the embeddings separately on more data without needing labels.
questions.explanation: The authors diagnose a data shortage, not a flaw of embeddings, and propose pretraining as the fix.

questions.question: Can you explain in your own words what CBOW predicts and what part of it we keep after training?
questions.answer: It predicts the middle word of a window from the surrounding words; we keep the learned embedding vectors.
questions.explanation: The page introduces CBOW; p.439 completes the description, and p.442 reuses only the embedding weights.
